messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the project Nicholas.  I've made only a small amount of progress, but I'm starting to get a hint of what you are attempting.

I learned your study area is ~340ha in size; a study area such as this would better be represented in units of UTMs; curvature of the earth is not going to matter for a study area of this size.

I am by no means clever about GIS systems, but one of the problems stems from latitude/longitude as the shapefile is organised, and metres for the projection.  Sometimes that works out, but more often than not is causes difficulties, and this is one of those cases.  When I produce a survey from my design criteria, the transect endpoint coordinates are produced in degrees

but the accompanying map uses UTM coordinates

rendering the resulting design invisible.

Moving on to the computed coverage probabilities; I saw your coverage grid also in units of degrees, spaced such that there are only 11 in the study area--that's really too few to get a good grasp of coverage.  On the other hand, from what I can tell looking at your map, these coverage grid points are ~350m apart.  If your sampler width is 282m, then placing a transect equidistant between any two coverage grid points will result in animals standing at either grid point to be "covered" detected.  Hence, for almost any design you place into that study area with a modest amount of effort, coverage probability will be uniformly high, if that is the true sampler width.  Consequently, your coverage map returns with all grid points covered all the time.  That's the explanation for the "binary" coverage probability you were experiencing.

I was able to achieve non-binary coverage probabilities by reducing survey effort (systematic parallel lines) to something on the order of 10km

My overall comments are:

- to use the design engine, you need not bring in the sightings and the tracks into Distance; they play no role in producing a survey design

- perform all your  cartographic transformations outside of Distance and use metres rather than degrees when in Distance

- your study area measures roughly 2.5km(NS) x 3.5km(EW), laying in ~20 transects systematically throughout the study area (sampling off trails) should be doable.

You can make inference where you did go, but not where you had no chance of going.

On Wednesday, March 14, 2001 at 3:13:40 PM UTC+7, Distance Development wrote:
> Hi Steve,
>
> I'm posting my reply to the distance-sampling list, as your question raises
> several points of general interest.  My answer is given below your message.
>
> On Wed, 14 Mar 2001 10:33:19 +1300, Steve Dawson wrote:
>
> > >Dear Len,
> > >
> > >I hope you don't mind if I ask you a question directly. I would very much
> > >appreciate your advice.
> > >
> > >With our latest data set (an aerial survey of dolphins) we've experimented
> > >with binnings to achieve the smoothest possible histogram, which, by
> > >intuition, should be the easiest to model. Having found "good" cutpoints,
> > >there seem to be two ways to use them in Distance (3.5):
> > >
> > >(1). In the "data filter", enter those as manual cutpoints in the
> > >"intervals" screen and group the data for analysis. This truncates the data
> > >past the last cutpoint. While doing this does throw some information away
> > >(the exact distance of each sighting), it does force the fitting process to
> > >use the "best" cutpoints.
> > >
> > >In our case doing this results in an ESW of 250.86m (CV=5.32%).
> > >
> > >(2). If we do not specify cutpoints in the "data filter", but choose a
> > >truncation level, then go to the "model" screen, choose "diagnostics" and
> > >"detection function" we can enter cutpoints to use for the GOF testing.
> > >
> > >Doing this results in an ESW of 240.50m (CV=5.98%).
> > >
> > >In "Distance" I have found little explicit advice on what to do. It says
> > >you can analyse data as grouped if they are problematic (i.e. show heaping
> > >or rounding), implying that if they are not problematic you should not
> > >group the data for analysis. Our data are not problematic, but with
> > >appropriate binning we can smooth the histogram considerably.
> > >
> > >It seems to me that what is happening at (1) is that we are forcing
> > >Distance to use those cutpoints to fit the detection function. If we choose
> > >(2), Distance chooses a set of arbitary cutpoints, and uses those to
> > >estimate the detection function, but then uses our cutpoints to evaluate
> > >GOF. It seems to my meagre brain that if by experimentation we have found
> > >really good cutpoints, we SHOULD use them, and take the approach in (1).
> > >
> > >What do you think?
> > >
> > >Cheers,
> > >
> > >________________
> > >Dr Steve Dawson, Senior Lecturer
> > >Trustee, New Zealand Whale and Dolphin Trust
> > >Marine Science Department, Otago University
> > >P.O. Box 56, Dunedin, New Zealand.
>
> Specifying interval cutpoints in the Data Filter has a different effect from
> specifying them in the Model Definition (under Detection Function |
> Diagnostics), and is used for a different reason.
>
> You choose intervals in the Data Filter if you want the data to be *analyzed*
> as interval (grouped/binned) data.  You would do this if (i) your data were
> actually collected in intervals, or (ii) you are trying to work around some
> problem in the data, such as evasive movement.
>
> If neither of these are the case, you are almost always better to leave your
> data as exact, and not put it into intervals for the analysis.  By putting
> your distances into intervals, you are throwing information away and may
> therefore get a less reliable result.  In many cases, you will get worse
> precision using intervals - but not in all cases.  It is quite possible to
> fiddle around with the cutpoints until you get a lower CV than in the exact
> data -- but are the results more reliable?  Doing an analysis 20 different
> ways and choosing the answer with the lowest CV is rarely the best policy.
> So, I believe its usually best to convert exact data into intervals only if
> you're trying to fix a specific problem.  Perhaps others have a different
> perspective on this?
>
> You choose interval cutpoints in the Model Definition (under Detection
> Function | Diagnostics) when your data is collected and analyzed as exact,
> and you want to fine-tune the goodness of fit histograms and tests that
> Distance produces.  Note that in this case, the data are *not changed* - they
> are analyzed as exact.  Only the histograms and the goodness of fit
> statistics are changed.  (You can easily confirm this for yourself in
> Distance -- try changing the cutpoints in Diagnostics and confirm that the
> estimated ESW doesn't change at all.)
>
> Note that if you define intervals in the Data Filter, then your data are
> already put into intervals by the time they arrive at the Model Definition.
> In this case, any intervals you specify in the Diagnostics page are ignored
> -- the intervals you get for histograms and goodness of fit are those you
> specified in the Data Filter.
>
> Why would you want to fiddle with the cutpoints for histograms and goodness-
> of-fit for your exact data?  Firstly, you would do this to look for potential
> problems in your data during exploratory data analysis.  For example, you can
> look for a spike at (or close) to 0 distance, by defining lots of small
> intervals at small distances (e.g., for a study with a truncation distance of
> 100 meters and lots of observations you could have cutpoints of 0, 1, 2, 3,
> 4, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100).  You can look for
> rounding by defining cutpoints that bracket the rounding peaks (e.g., if you
> suspect rounding to the nearest 10 meters, define cutpoints of 0, 1, 9, 11,
> 19, 21, 29, 31, etc).  You get the idea: you're looking for potential
> problems with the distance data, and defining the cutpoints so as to best
> help you identify and diagnose them.
>
> The second reason for changing cutpoints in Diagnostics is to make a nicer
> detection function for putting in your publication.  I would almost always
> recommend putting a figure showing the data and fitted detection function in
> any publication that uses distance sampling.  In this case, you don't want
> nearly as many cutpoints as in the exploratory phase, but you may not want
> the equal cutpoints that Distance gives by default either.  For example, you
> could have larger cutpoint intervals further from the line, where there are
> less data and the fit is not so critical (one rule of thumb is to choose
> cutpoints such that the number of observations in each interval is similar).
> I don't have a strong opinion about how histograms should look in
> publications -- perhaps others do?
>
> Of course, how you define intervals for your histogram will also affect the
> chi-sq goodness-of-fit statistic you get out.  This is great in the
> exploratory phase, but seems a bit of a shame in the confirmation/publication
> phase -- when refereeing a publication you may suspect that the authors have
> manipulated their intervals to get the best possible goodness-of-fit, and
> hide any problems! On a less paranoid level, it is rather arbitrary.  In a
> future version of Distance, we hope to add Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von
> Mises goodness-of-fit statistics to the list -- both of these can be applied
> to continuous as well as discrete data, so for exact distances they won't be
> affected by the histogram bins.
>
> Hope this helps,
>
>  - Len
>
>
> --

> Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews

messages.body_plain:
Thinh

The histograms displayed show three different sets of cutpoints for exact data and are linked to the chi-square goodness of fit tests that follow the plots.  Chi-square tests are dependent upon the cutpoints used.  Because Distance does not know what set of cutpoints is appropriate (because the user did not specify cutpoints using Model Definition | Detection Function | Diagnostics) it provides three.  They are all of the same detection function, simply depicting the histogram differently.

To prevent this confusion, specify the cutpoints most appropriate for your data using the Model Definition | Detection Function | Diagnostics.  Distance will then produce only plot (and associated chi-square test) associated with that set of cutpoints.

Hi James,

I am dealing with data from a similar set up (collected via cruise ships) ad was kindly directed to a few resources and given some important bits of advice. I'll link to/paste the responses I got below for your reference as well.

Hope these are helpful to you,

>From Eric Rexstad:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/distance-sampling/ZakrkcgpMs4/nvamOCGPEQAJ

>From Rob Williams:
There isn’t a transect per se in a platform of opportunity study. Instead, you divide your effort into roughly evenly sized segments. Then, you can specify the size of a moving block (# of segments) to use in DSM in Distance to estimate variance. If you are doing this in R, you have more options for estimating variance. If you like, you can try setting each trip as a resampling unit with a bootstrap or jackknife. We tried that with Antarctic cruise ships:

http://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol11/iss1/art1/

The newer variance propagation methods based on segments are now integrated into Distance, and they don’t require you to specify a resampling unit. They do require a bunch of work to divide your tracks into segments that are short enough to have environmental conditions remain more or less constant along the segment, and long enough so that you don’t have a major problem with over dispersion. You wouldn’t want 100,000, 1km segments that had 99,950 zeroes and 50 ones.
http://www.nature.com/articles/srep04170
https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Alexandre_Zerbini/publication/50347370_Chilean_Blue_Whales_as_a_Case_Study_to_Illustrate_Methods_to_Estimate_Abundance_and_Evaluate_Conservation_Status_of_Rare_Species/links/09e4150f4f39f662a4000000.pdf

The best primer for this is David Miller’s recent review of DSM: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12105/abstract  No doubt you’ve read this already.

messages.subject: Re: Covariate model with missing observations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Olivier,

I am not on the Distance team but do have a fair bit of experience fitting detection functions with the R packages. My experience matches yours: ds() and ddf() will fail if the value of a detection function covariate is NA.

The problem of missing values is common to many types of models, not just detection functions, and as far as I know the Distance packages do not provide any special magic for dealing with this generic problem. I think you are left with the usual options you have when faced with the "missing data" problem elsewhere. For example, as you mentioned, you could invent a new factor level of "unknown" to go with "male" and "female". Or, prior to fitting detection functions, you could use other covariates or some external data to model or guess the sex of records that don't have it. Or remove sex as a covariate from your detection function. Or fit two detection functions: one with sex for the records that have it, and one without sex for the records that don't. Etc.

These are all solutions you could imagine when faced with missing data in other situations, e.g. when fitting a linear regression model, and I'm sure you have thought of them already. If someone knows of techniques specifically for dealing with missing values for detection functions, I'd be very interested to hear about them!

All the best,

Jason

Olivier

Sorry for the slow response, I was travelling last week.  I performed an experiment using the "minke" dataset that is included in the Distance package.  That dataset contains several transects with no sightings (distances recorded as NA), but no covariates.  Consequently, I manufactured a covariate to see if I could get `ds()` to use that covariate in the detection function when there were transects without sightings.

library(Distance)
data(minke)
eric <- minke  # my toy copy
eric$cov <- runif(min = 0.01, max = 1, n=99)
trouble <- ds(data=eric, key="hn", formula=~cov)
real <- ds(data=eric, key="hn")
summary(trouble)
plot(trouble)
summarize_ds_models(real, trouble, output="plain")
eric.covNA <- eric  # another copy
eric.covNA$cov <- ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(eric.covNA$distance), NA, eric.covNA$cov)
real.trouble <- ds(data=eric.covNA, key="hn", formula=~cov)
summarize_ds_models(real, trouble, real.trouble, output="plain")

I produce identical results (see summarize_ds_models() results) whether I set the covariate on empty transects to NA or to random values; the covariate value is ignored when distance=NA (i.e. empty transects).  Note in this toy example, the covariate is continuous rather than discrete as in your case.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Bit of an off topic question, but I was looking for ways to determine trends in my time series data and came across the GAM models in the Advanced Distance Methods book. I have been following the paper of Fewster et al. (2000) and have reached a point where I am stuck.

I want to determine the significance of the trend in my data. The paper says I should use the bootstrapped confidence intervals to find the percentage population change between any two years. But the steps outlined in the bootstrapping suggest that I should resample sites (in my case transects) and set the size of the sample to the number of sites (transects), then fit a GAM to this sample. I am confused by this as I understand this as bootstrapping a sample of my transects in a given year, and then applying a GAM to this sample. But if the sample contains only data from one year's sites then how can I apply a GAM to this (it won't be a time series).

I initially tried something different, in that I took bootstrap samples of the data points in my time series (size = # years, replace = T). Then, from what I could understand from the description in the paper, I fitted a GAM to the new sample and then calculated the percentage population change between the oldest and newest data points (ex. % difference between density in 2010 and in 2016). Was I perhaps correct in this first approach?

As this paper is now a bit older, are there also perhaps more simplified approaches to determine the significance of a trend in GAM models? I am using the gam function in the mgcv package, and this package now creates confidence intervals itself, rather than requiring them to be made manually as described by Fewster et al.

Thanks!!!
Steve
